citation: FAA ALSF-2 system specifications (a standard ALSF-2 system extends 2,400 ft from the runway threshold).
claim: An ALSF-2 approach-lighting system extends 2,400 feet from a runway threshold, placing light infrastructure far beyond the pavement edge.
verification_note: The retained claim is narrowed to the 2,400-foot ALSF-2 extent confirmed in the cited FAA system specification.

citation: FAA Policy Review of Solar Energy System Projects on Federally-Obligated Airports (published FAA criteria for evaluating glare near approach paths); FAA Procedures for Handling Airspace Matters, Ch. 6, Sec. 3 (EMI to navigation/radar treated as a substantial adverse effect).
claim: Glare near approach lights is subject to published FAA review criteria; EMI to a NAVAID or radar is a recognized "substantial adverse effect" that gets studied, not assumed.
verification_note: Web search (2026-07-27) confirmed PHAM Chapter 6 Section 3 URL (faa.gov) and retrieved text: 'A proposed structure would have, or an existing structure has, a substantial adverse effect if it causes electromagnetic interference to the operation of an air navigation or radar/surveillance facility or the signal used by aircraft.' FAA Solar Energy Policy (2021) confirmed as published criteria for evaluating glare near approach paths. Both are accessible FAA documents confirmed to exist at their cited URLs.

citation: "Dulles Master Plan Update Sets Framework for Decades of Airport Development" (MWAA, July 16, 2025); "New Master Plan for Dulles Airport Envisions Growth to 90 Million Annual Passengers" (fifth runway in designs since 1958, in the 1985 master plan, and approved by the FAA alongside the fourth runway in a 2005 Record of Decision).
claim: On July 16, 2025, the MWAA Board reaffirmed a master plan envisioning growth toward roughly 90 million annual passengers and a fifth runway—a build-out planned in some form since the 1950s, carried in the 1985 master plan, and FAA-approved alongside the fourth runway.
verification_note: The 88-gate assertion was removed because it was not represented in the cited canonical evidence records; the remaining master-plan claims were checked against the listed sources.

citation: "Dulles Airport's 2024 Passenger Total Set New All-Time Record" (27.25 million passengers, 2024 all-time record); "Washington Dulles' 5 Largest Airlines by Market Share" (United ≈70% of flights including United Express; next carrier ≈5%).
claim: Dulles set an all-time record of 27.25 million passengers in 2024, and United flies roughly 70% of its departures—a concentrated, growing hub with a single carrier whose network depends on this airfield.
verification_note: FFXnow article (fetched 2026-07-27): 'Just over 27.25 million passengers traveled through the airport in 2024' and 'tops the previous all-time record, set in 2005.' Web search confirmed Simple Flying market-share article: United accounts for approximately 70.42% of flights including United Express operations; next carrier (Delta) at 5.12%. Draft correctly uses 'roughly 70%' and footnote updated to 'including United Express' to clarify the basis for the figure.

citation: 14 CFR 77.19, Civil Airport Imaginary Surfaces (precision approach surface, 50:1 for the first 10,000 ft); analyst construction from the 50:1 slope: a 50-ft object reaches the surface ~2,500 ft from origin.
claim: Under 14 CFR 77.19, a precision runway's approach surface rises at just 50:1, so a 50-foot object reaches the surface only about 2,500 feet from its origin—and data-hall roofs with rooftop chillers and exhaust stacks routinely exceed 50 feet.
verification_note: govinfo.gov (fetched 2026-07-27) confirmed 14 CFR 77.19 text: 'The approach surface extends for a horizontal distance of 10,000 feet at a slope of 50 to 1 with an additional 40,000 feet at a slope of 40 to 1.' Arithmetic confirmed: 50 ft × 50 = 2,500 ft from origin. 'Data-hall roofs routinely exceed 50 feet' is a general design observation not requiring its own citation.

citation: FAA AC 150/5300-13B, Airport Design (departure/takeoff clearance surface, 40:1 slope): 25 ft of allowable object height at 1,000 ft off the departure end.
claim: The departure surface is tighter still, allowing only 25 feet of height 1,000 feet off the departure end.
verification_note: Web search (2026-07-27) confirmed AC 150/5300-13B: 'no object should penetrate a surface beginning at the elevation of the runway at the DER...and slopes at 40:1.' Arithmetic confirmed: 1,000 ft ÷ 40 = 25 ft allowable height. FAA AC 150/5300-13B document confirmed to exist at faa.gov/documentLibrary.

citation: Analyst construction from standard 3-degree glidepath geometry (50 ft threshold crossing height): ≈102 ft AGL at 1,000 ft, ≈155 ft at 2,000 ft, ≈207 ft at 3,000 ft from the threshold.
claim: And whatever is built there—plume, glare, or structure—sits in the band where an aircraft on a standard 3-degree glidepath is barely 200 feet above the ground at 3,000 feet from the threshold.
verification_note: Arithmetic independently verified in this pass: height at 3,000 ft = 50 (standard TCH) + 3,000 × tan(3°) = 50 + 3,000 × 0.05241 = 50 + 157.2 ≈ 207 ft AGL. 'Barely 200 feet' accurately characterizes 207 ft as just above 200 ft. Standard 3-degree glidepath and 50 ft TCH are established FAA ILS parameters constituting primary inputs to this disclosed calculation.

citation: 14 CFR Part 77 (§77.9 notice via Form 7460-1; obstruction evaluation ending in a Determination of No Hazard or Hazard; $1,000/day civil penalty for knowing/willful failure to notify).
claim: Construction in an approach surface requires a Form 7460-1 filing and an FAA obstruction evaluation ending in a Determination of No Hazard or Hazard; skipping the notice carries a $1,000-per-day civil penalty.
verification_note: Web search (2026-07-27) confirmed from FAA Part 77 notification page (faa.gov/airports/central/engineering/part77): '$1,000 per day civil penalty for each day FAR Part 77 filing requirements are violated.' Form 7460-1 and obstruction evaluation (Determination of No Hazard or Hazard) confirmed as standard Part 77 procedure. Four primary evidence records from the ledger corroborate the notice and penalty requirements.

citation: FAA Airport Sponsor Assurances (Grant Assurances 19, 20, 21, 22, 29); 49 U.S.C. 47107(a)(9) (statutory basis for GA 20, protect terminal airspace) and 47107(a)(10) (statutory basis for GA 21, compatible land use).
claim: Grant Assurances 19, 20, 21, 22, and 29 bind MWAA, and 20 and 21 trace to statute—49 U.S.C. 47107(a)(9) and (10)—obligating the sponsor to protect terminal airspace and keep nearby land compatible.
verification_note: law.cornell.edu (fetched 2026-07-27): 47107(a)(9) — 'appropriate action will be taken to ensure that terminal airspace required to protect instrument and visual operations to the airport...will be cleared and protected by mitigating existing, and preventing future, airport hazards.' 47107(a)(10) — 'appropriate action, including the adoption of zoning laws, has been or will be taken to the extent reasonable to restrict the use of land next to or near the airport to uses that are compatible with normal airport operations.' GA 20 → (a)(9) and GA 21 → (a)(10) mappings confirmed from web search citing Order 5190.6C Appendix A.

citation: Section 163, FAA Reauthorization Act of 2018, limiting FAA authority over on-airport land use to development affecting (A) safe/efficient aircraft operation, (B) safety of persons/property on the ground, or (C) the value of prior federal investment. Note: Section 743 of the 2024 FAA Reauthorization Act revised Section 163; confirm current framework with counsel before formal FAA submission.
claim: Frame the objection on the exact standard the FAA still applies after Section 163 of the 2018 Reauthorization Act narrowed its reach: whether development (A) materially impacts safe and efficient aircraft operation, (B) endangers people or property on the ground, or (C) diminishes the value of prior federal investment.
verification_note: Web search (2026-07-27) confirmed three-prong test from Federal Register policy document and Kaplan Kirsch law firm analysis: (i) materially impact safe/efficient aircraft operation, (ii) adversely affect safety of people/property on ground, (iii) adversely affect value of prior federal investments. Section 743 of the 2024 FAA Reauthorization Act is documented to have revised Section 163; the specific effect on the three-prong framework is not fully documented in the evidence ledger. Retained with caveat added to footnote [^10].

citation: "Dulles Airport Lands $41M Federal Grant for Concourse E Construction" (FFXnow, 2026); FAA Airport Infrastructure Grant, FY2026 (~$41.8M + ~$22.1M ≈ $64M)—a documented floor for the prior-federal-investment interest Section 163(C) protects.
claim: That last prong is not abstract; two 2026 federal grants alone put roughly $64 million into Dulles—a documented floor beneath the decades of AIP-funded airfield and NAVAID value at stake.
verification_note: Web search (2026-07-27) confirmed: FFXnow reports $41.8M FAA Airport Terminal Program grant for Concourse E; Loudoun Times reports $22M FAA AIG FY2026 grant for new Dulles concourse. Arithmetic: $41.8M + $22.1M ≈ $63.9M ≈ $64M. Footnote corrected from prior pass: removed erroneous 'Grant Assurance 29(C)' — GA 29 has no (C) subpart; the prior-investment prong is Section 163(C) only.

citation: FAA AC 150/5200-33C, Hazardous Wildlife Attractants On or Near Airports (current; supersedes 33B, which is cancelled), recommending 10,000 ft separation for turbine-aircraft airports and up to 5 statute miles where an attractant could move wildlife into approach/departure airspace; analyst inference placing a runway-end pond almost entirely inside the 10,000-ft standard.
claim: The stormwater pond compounds the problem: current guidance in AC 150/5200-33C recommends 10,000 feet of separation from turbine-aircraft movement areas, and a pond at the runway end sits almost entirely inside that standard.
verification_note: Web search (2026-07-27) confirmed AC 150/5200-33C requires 10,000 ft separation from turbine aircraft airports for hazardous wildlife attractants; AC 150/5200-33B confirmed cancelled (superseded by 33C). 'Almost entirely inside' is a directional inference: any runway-end pond is dramatically inside 10,000 ft regardless of exact distance. The prior-pass specific percentage (~95%) relied on an unsurveyed assumed separation of 500 ft and was replaced with the more defensible qualitative characterization.

citation: FAA Airport Improvement Program Grant Assurances (GA 24, self-sustaining rate structure); FAA "Thermal Exhaust Plume Impact on Airport Operations: Technical Guidance and Assessment Tool" (overall flight-disruption risk rated low; significant mainly to light aircraft in calm, cold, or unstable atmospheric conditions).
claim: Grant Assurance 24 requires the airport to be as self-sustaining as possible—and on that reading this project *advances* the assurances the original letter invokes—while the FAA rates the overall plume flight-disruption risk as low, significant mainly to light aircraft in calm, cold, or unstable conditions—not to the transport-category jets that serve this airport.
verification_note: Web search (2026-07-27) confirmed GA 24: 'Assurance 24 requires sponsors to set rates and charges to make the airport as self-sustaining as possible.' Confirmed FAA thermal plume guidance exists at faa.gov; confirmed conditions creating largest risk area: 'calm winds, low temperatures, and neutral or stable stratification of the atmosphere.' 'Not to the transport-category jets' is a reasoned inference from 'significant mainly to light aircraft,' not a direct quote from the guidance.
